evidence_quotes.quote: However, there is an overrepresentation of the Black population in unsanitary housing conditions, since 61% of the population without access to water supply was Black and only 37% was white; 67% of the population without access to waste collection was Black and only 30% was white; 58% of the population without access to sewage treatment was Black and 40% was white; and 76% of the population without a bathroom was Black and only 20% was white.

In addition, I analyze current data on access to sanitation and morbidity/mortality due to diseases related to inadequate environmental sanitation by color/race, based on databases of the IBGE’s 2010 Census and of Tabnet DataSUS, from SUS.

Institutional racism, also known as systemic racism, corresponds to the structural mechanism of selective racial exclusion in the access to benefits generated from the State and enjoyed by privileged racial groups.

That is because, by neglecting the racial variable as a factor of inequality and a criterion for allocating public policies, racial inequalities remain unmeasured, thereby unaddressed, perpetuating and rendering invisible the colonial continuum of production and reproduction of institutional racism in its various facets.

This article was originally published in Saúde e Sociedade journal (v. 29, n. 2, e180519) in 2020, based on research funded by the Conselho Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico (CNPq).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household basic sanitation service access in Brazil, specifically access to potable water supply, solid waste collection, sewage treatment/disposal, and presence of a household bathroom.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/literal broad wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper arguably passes (plain=yes -> plain_criterion2_decision='include') because its central sociological and political-historical thesis examines institutional racism, state 'negligence'/omission in urban planning and sanitation policy, non-enforcement of constitutional and statutory sanitation guarantees (Law 11.445/2007, Law 12.288/2010, and PNSIPN 2013), and the failure to use race as a planning criterion in public policy allocation. Under the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, however, Criterion 2 is NOT met (narrow=no): empirically, the study only cross-tabulates national aggregate Census sanitation deficits and DataSUS mortality/hospitalization counts by self-declared color/race (Black vs. white), treating colonial continuity, institutional racism, and state omission as macro-governance/structural background rather than examining any specific rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Combines exploratory bibliographic/historical research with descriptive secondary quantitative analysis of Brazil's 2010 IBGE Demographic Census (sanitation inadequacy by race/color) and Ministry of Health DataSUS records (1996-2014 mortality and 2008-2016 hospitalizations for diseases related to inadequate environmental sanitation by race/color).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household-level population proportions and absolute counts lacking water supply (relying on wells, springs, water trucks, rainwater, rivers, etc.), lacking solid waste collection, lacking sewage treatment (relying on septic tanks, rudimentary cesspools, ditches, rivers, etc.), and lacking a bathroom in the home (Figure 1, pp. 11-12), alongside health morbidity/mortality outcomes (DRSAI).
criterion_notes.c5: Population (Brazilian population disaggregated by self-declared Black [Black + Mixed] and white color/race in national IBGE Census and DataSUS records), empirical stratifier/exposure (race/color framed conceptually via macro-historical institutional and environmental racism), outcomes (lack of water supply, waste collection, sewage treatment, and household bathroom; DRSAI mortality and hospitalizations), and study design (exploratory bibliographic/historical review plus descriptive cross-sectional secondary analysis of national census and health administrative data) are identifiable, making clear that no rule-type legal/administrative exposure is analyzed.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (an invited 2026 English translation of a 2020 Portuguese article, with abstracts in English, Spanish, and Portuguese).

study_design: Exploratory bibliographic/historical review combined with descriptive cross-sectional secondary quantitative analysis of national census (IBGE 2010) and administrative health (DataSUS 1996-2016) databases
population_and_sample: Brazilian population in the 2010 IBGE Demographic Census (comparing Black [51%] and white [48%] residents at the national aggregate level) and national DataSUS mortality (1996-2014, N = 231,087 DRSAI deaths) and hospitalization records (Jan 2008-Oct 2016)
exposure: Self-declared race/color (Black [Black + Mixed] vs. white), interpreted conceptually through colonial continuity, macro-level institutional/environmental racism, and state policy omission (no rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism measured)
outcome: Lack of access to potable water supply, solid waste collection, sewage treatment, and a household bathroom (2010 IBGE Census), plus mortality (1996-2014) and hospitalizations (2008-2016) from diseases related to inadequate environmental sanitation (DRSAI)
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope of Criterion 2. While the paper reports national descriptive statistics from Brazil's 2010 IBGE Census on racial disparities in household access to water supply, waste collection, sewage treatment, and bathrooms (as well as 1996-2016 DataSUS morbidity/mortality from sanitation-related diseases), the only empirical exposure/stratifier analyzed is self-declared race/color. Institutional racism, environmental racism, colonial continuity, and state omission/non-enforcement of constitutional and statutory frameworks (Law 11.445/2007, Law 12.288/2010, PNSIPN 2013) are discussed as macro-governance and historical-sociological framing rather than analyzed as a specific rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism governing service access (e.g., eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs, administrative burden, enforcement, or utility structure). Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper's sustained political-historical focus on institutional racism and state policy omission would arguably qualify (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include'). Note for corpus deduplication: Footnote 1 (PDF Page 1) and the Acknowledgements (PDF Page 22) state that this 2026 article is an invited English translation of an article originally published in Portuguese in Saúde e Sociedade (2020, v. 29, n. 2, e180519).
